entries.definition: Ending contact with someone suddenly and without explanation, usually by ignoring all of their messages and calls.
examples: We had three great dates, and then he started ghosting me.
Ghosting might feel easier, but a short honest message is kinder.

entries.definition: Sending occasional flirty but noncommittal messages to keep someone interested without any real intention of pursuing a relationship.
examples: A heart emoji every two weeks isn't interest — it's breadcrumbing.

entries.definition: Cutting off direct contact with someone while still watching, liking or reacting to their social media posts.
examples: She stopped replying months ago but still views every story — classic orbiting.

entries.definition: When someone who previously ghosted you reappears and acts as if nothing happened.
examples: Six months of silence, then a 'hey stranger' text? That's zombieing.

entries.definition: Keeping someone as a backup option — interested enough to stay in touch, but not enough to commit — while pursuing other people.
examples: He only texts when his other plans fall through; I think I'm being benched.

entries.definition: The colder months of the year, when single people are said to look for a partner to settle down with for companionship.
examples: It's October, so cuffing season has officially begun.

entries.definition: In a committed relationship, especially one that began during cuffing season.
examples: Don't bother inviting him out — he's cuffed now.

entries.definition: Charm or skill in attracting a romantic interest. A shortening of the middle of the word 'charisma'.
examples: He got her number in two minutes — that's serious rizz.
Unspoken rizz is when you charm someone without saying a word.
entries.note: Named Oxford Word of the Year in 2023.

entries.definition: A person who has a lot of rizz; someone notably good at flirting.
examples: Everyone at the party wanted to talk to him — total rizzler.

entries.definition: Someone who goes to excessive lengths to win the favour of a person they are attracted to, often without the feelings being returned.
examples: He drove two hours to bring her coffee — she called him a simp, but she smiled.

entries.definition: A photo or post deliberately designed to attract attention, compliments or romantic interest.
examples: Posting a gym selfie at midnight? That's a thirst trap.

entries.definition: To make a bold attempt to tell someone you are interested in them, accepting the risk of rejection.
examples: Life is short — just shoot your shot and ask her out.

entries.definition: A friend who helps you approach, talk to or impress a romantic interest. Also wingwoman or wingperson.
examples: My wingman kept the conversation going while I worked up the courage to say hi.

entries.definition: A person who spends time with a couple and feels left out or unneeded.
examples: I love them both, but being the third wheel at dinner was awkward.

entries.definition: A situation in which one person wants a romantic relationship but the other sees them only as a friend.
examples: He said I'm like a sister to him — I've been friend-zoned.

entries.definition: Keeping a partner hidden from your friends, family and social media, often for months.
examples: We've dated for a year and I've never met his friends. Am I being pocketed?

entries.definition: Another word for pocketing: deliberately keeping a relationship secret from the people in your life.
examples: She's not shy — she's stashing you.

entries.definition: Short for 'delusional'; playfully describes holding unrealistic hopes about a crush or relationship.
examples: He liked one photo and I'm planning our wedding. I'm so delulu.

entries.definition: A sudden feeling of repulsion toward someone you were attracted to, often triggered by something small or silly.
examples: He clapped when the plane landed and I instantly got the ick.

entries.definition: An affectionate name for a romantic partner. Often said to stand for 'before anyone else', though it most likely began as a shortening of 'babe'.
examples: Movie night with bae tonight.

entries.definition: An affectionate term for a boyfriend, girlfriend or partner.
examples: She's spending the weekend with her boo.

entries.definition: Turning down someone's romantic interest indirectly, for example with vague, delayed or one-word replies.
examples: Every time I suggest a date she says 'maybe' — I'm getting curved.

entries.definition: Wanting two people, real or fictional, to be in a relationship. From 'relationship'.
examples: The whole office is shipping the two new hires.

entries.definition: 'One True Pairing': your favourite couple, real or fictional.
examples: My grandparents are my OTP.

entries.definition: Keeping other romantic prospects flirtatiously on hand while in a relationship, as an emotional cushion in case it ends.
examples: Still texting your exes 'just in case' is cushioning.

entries.definition: The group of people someone is casually dating or talking to at the same time.
examples: She's not ready to commit — she's still managing her roster.

entries.definition: When someone appears in your dating life only during the sunny months, then disappears when the weather turns.
examples: He shows up every June and vanishes by September — freckling.

entries.definition: Being completely upfront from the start about what you want from dating, whether that is marriage or something casual.
examples: She was hardballing on the first date: 'I want kids within five years.'

entries.definition: Standing someone up for a date and then blocking them on every app so they cannot get in touch.
examples: I waited at the restaurant for an hour — he'd cloaked me.

entries.definition: A person's primary or most important romantic partner.
examples: Let me introduce you to my main squeeze.

entries.definition: To behave playfully toward someone in a way that shows romantic interest; also a person who does this often.
examples: They flirted all evening over board games.
He's a terrible flirt — he compliments everyone.

entries.definition: A playful, quick-witted exchange of teasing remarks.
examples: Their banter was so natural it felt like they'd known each other for years.

entries.definition: A prepared opening line intended to start a romantic conversation, often cheesy or humorous.
examples: 'Are you a parking ticket? Because you've got 'fine' written all over you' is a classic pickup line.

entries.definition: A remark, question or activity used to start a conversation and ease initial awkwardness.
examples: Asking about the book she was reading was the perfect icebreaker.

entries.definition: The first thing you say to start a conversation with someone you're interested in.
examples: A genuine question about their dog is a better opener than any line.

entries.definition: Holding eye contact a moment longer than usual to signal interest.
examples: A lingering gaze across the room said more than words could.

entries.definition: Lighthearted, affectionate joking at someone's expense that creates playful tension. It should always feel kind, never hurtful.
examples: She teased him about his terrible dance moves — then asked him to dance.

entries.definition: To briefly close one eye as a playful, often flirtatious, signal.
examples: He winked as he handed her the coffee.

entries.definition: The quality of being pleasant, delightful and attractive in a way that wins people over.
examples: His easy charm put everyone at ease.

entries.definition: A compelling attractiveness or presence that draws others in.
examples: She has the kind of charisma that fills a room.

entries.definition: Pretending to be shy or modest in a playful, flirtatious way.
examples: She gave him a coy smile and looked away.

entries.definition: Deliberately acting uninterested or unavailable to make yourself seem more desirable.
examples: Is she busy all week, or is she playing hard to get?

entries.definition: Subconsciously or subtly copying another person's posture, gestures or tone, which can signal and build rapport.
examples: When she leaned in, he leaned in too — natural mirroring.

entries.definition: Alternating between signals of interest and signals of distance to create excitement or intrigue.
examples: 'You're cute — too bad you like pineapple on pizza' is a push-pull line.

entries.definition: Referring back to an earlier joke or shared moment in a conversation, building a sense of connection.
examples: Bringing up the 'emergency penguin' joke from their first date always made her laugh.

entries.definition: Uncrossed arms, relaxed posture and facing someone directly — nonverbal signs of interest and approachability.
examples: She turned her whole body toward him: open body language.

entries.definition: A person who is confident, suave and skilled at charming others.
examples: He ordered her favourite drink before she arrived — smooth operator.

entries.definition: Charming, confident and elegant in manner.
examples: He looked suave in his tailored suit.

entries.definition: To try to win someone's love or affection, especially with the aim of a relationship.
examples: He wooed her with handwritten letters.

entries.definition: Taking action to show romantic interest, such as asking someone out or leaning in for a kiss.
examples: They'd been friends for years before he finally made a move.

entries.definition: Starting a conversation with a stranger you're interested in, without any prior introduction.
examples: A cold approach at a bookshop is braver than any dating app message.

entries.definition: Approaching someone you share some context with — a mutual friend, class or hobby.
examples: Meeting through her running club made it a warm approach.

entries.definition: Showing quick, clever and inventive humour.
examples: Her witty replies made texting her addictive.

entries.definition: Dressing or behaving flamboyantly to attract attention, like a peacock showing its feathers.
examples: The sequined jacket was pure peacocking.

entries.definition: Freely given, enthusiastic and ongoing agreement. Good flirting always respects it, and it can be withdrawn at any time.
examples: He asked 'Can I kiss you?' — consent is attractive.

entries.definition: Being turned down after expressing romantic interest. Handling it gracefully is a sign of maturity.
examples: He took the rejection well and they stayed friends.

entries.definition: Of a line or gesture: corny, overly sentimental or obviously rehearsed — sometimes endearingly so.
examples: The pun was so cheesy she couldn't stop laughing.

entries.definition: To flutter your eyelashes, often exaggeratedly, as a playful flirting gesture.
examples: She batted her eyelashes and asked him to carry the shopping.

entries.definition: When someone opens your message, so you can see they've read it, but doesn't reply.
examples: I asked him out three hours ago and I've been left on read.

entries.definition: Someone whose messages are short, bland and give you little to respond to.
examples: 'k.' 'lol.' 'nice.' — he's such a dry texter.

entries.definition: Sending another message before the other person has replied to your first one.
examples: Is double texting desperate, or just enthusiastic?

entries.definition: A person who creates a fake online identity to deceive someone into a relationship; also the act of doing so.
examples: He refused every video call — turns out he was a catfish.

entries.definition: Presenting a flattering but misleading version of yourself online, such as using very old photos or exaggerating your height.
examples: His profile photos were from ten years ago — mild kittenfishing.

entries.definition: Hinting at a new relationship on social media without fully revealing your partner — a hand in a photo, two coffee cups.
examples: A mystery hand holding a wine glass? She's soft launching someone.

entries.definition: Openly announcing a relationship on social media with clear photos of your partner.
examples: After the soft launch came the hard launch: a full couple's selfie.

entries.definition: To send someone a private message on social media to express romantic interest.
examples: He slid into her DMs with a comment about her travel photos.

entries.definition: To signal interest in someone's profile on a dating app; swiping left means passing.
examples: I swiped right because of his dog, honestly.

entries.definition: On a dating app, a connection made when two people both express interest in each other.
examples: We matched on Sunday and met for coffee on Wednesday.

entries.definition: To remove a connection on a dating app, ending the ability to message each other.
examples: His first message was rude, so I unmatched.

entries.definition: The short self-description on a dating or social media profile.
examples: Her bio said 'will judge you by your taco order'.

entries.definition: A question on a dating profile that you answer to show your personality and give others something to message you about.
examples: His profile prompt answer about his grandmother's cooking made me smile.

entries.definition: The indicator that shows someone is writing a reply — often watched with great anticipation.
examples: The typing bubble appeared and disappeared three times. Torture.

entries.definition: A message sent first thing in the day, often seen as a sweet sign someone is thinking about you.
examples: Getting a good morning text from him made her whole day.

entries.definition: Sending someone small things — memes, songs, funny videos — as a low-effort but meaningful sign of affection.
examples: She sends me a cat video every morning; that's pebbling.
entries.note: Named after penguins that give pebbles to potential mates.

entries.definition: 'What (are) you doing?' — a casual text often used to open a conversation or test the waters.
examples: A 'wyd' at 11 p.m. is rarely about what you're doing.

entries.definition: 'Hit me up' — an invitation to get in touch.
examples: Free this weekend, hmu.

entries.definition: Quietly, secretly or to a modest degree.
examples: I lowkey have a crush on my lab partner.

entries.definition: Openly and obviously; the opposite of lowkey.
examples: I highkey want him to ask me out.

entries.definition: The early period of getting to know someone romantically, before dating seriously or becoming exclusive.
examples: We're still in the talking stage — no labels yet.

entries.definition: A romantic connection that has some features of a relationship but has never been clearly defined or labelled.
examples: We spend every weekend together but won't call it dating. It's a situationship.

entries.definition: 'Define the relationship': the conversation where two people decide what they are to each other.
examples: After three months, it was time for the DTR talk.

entries.definition: Agreeing to date only each other, even if not yet using labels like boyfriend or girlfriend.
examples: We decided to be exclusive and deleted our dating apps.

entries.definition: Formally agreeing to be in a relationship, and often telling friends or posting about it.
examples: They made it official on their six-month anniversary.

entries.definition: The first planned romantic outing between two people.
examples: For our first date we went to a tiny dumpling place.

entries.definition: The early stage of a relationship when everything feels exciting, effortless and intensely romantic.
examples: They're in the honeymoon phase — they can't stop smiling at each other.

entries.definition: A relationship between partners who live far apart. Often abbreviated LDR.
examples: Video calls kept their long-distance relationship alive.

entries.definition: A romance that develops gradually, with attraction building over a long time.
examples: Their story was a slow burn: three years of friendship before the first kiss.

entries.definition: A relationship with constant flirting that never quite develops into dating.
examples: We've had a flirtationship since freshman year.

entries.definition: A romance between two people who were friends first.
examples: Their friends-to-lovers story started in kindergarten.

entries.definition: The yearly — or for new couples, monthly — return of a significant date in a relationship.
examples: For their first anniversary they returned to the café where they met.

entries.definition: A formal agreement to marry; the period between a proposal and the wedding.
examples: They announced their engagement at the family dinner.

entries.definition: The end of a romantic relationship.
examples: The breakup was mutual, but it still hurt.

entries.definition: Describes a relationship in which a couple repeatedly breaks up and gets back together.
examples: Their on-again, off-again romance lasted all of college.

entries.definition: A relationship that starts soon after a breakup, often before the person has fully moved on.
examples: I worried I was just his rebound.

entries.definition: Dating without expectations of commitment or exclusivity.
examples: She's just casual dating while she finishes her degree.

entries.definition: In a serious, dedicated relationship with long-term intentions.
examples: They've been in a committed relationship for five years.

entries.definition: The milestone of being introduced to a partner's family, often a sign the relationship is getting serious.
examples: Meeting the parents went well — her dad even laughed at my joke.

entries.definition: A warning sign that a person or relationship may be unhealthy or incompatible with you.
examples: Being rude to the waiter on a first date is a red flag.

entries.definition: A positive sign that someone is emotionally healthy, respectful or a good match.
examples: He remembered my sister's name — green flag.

entries.definition: A quirk that is neither good nor bad — just a little odd or surprising.
examples: She names all her houseplants. Beige flag, but I kind of love it.

entries.definition: Overwhelming someone with excessive affection, gifts and attention early on, often as a way to gain control.
examples: Flowers every day and 'I love you' after a week felt less romantic and more like love bombing.

entries.definition: Manipulating someone into doubting their own memory, perception or judgement.
examples: He kept insisting I'd imagined the argument — that's gaslighting.
entries.note: Named after the 1938 play 'Gas Light' and its 1944 film adaptation.

entries.definition: Giving backhanded compliments designed to lower someone's confidence and make them seek approval.
examples: 'You're pretty for someone who doesn't wear makeup' is negging, not flirting.

entries.definition: Behaviour that sends contradictory messages about someone's interest, leaving you unsure where you stand.
examples: He holds my hand, then doesn't text for days. So many mixed signals.

entries.definition: Alternating unpredictably between being very affectionate and distant.
examples: She's so hot and cold I never know which version I'll get.

entries.definition: Making promises about a shared future, like trips or moving in, to win someone over now, with no real intention of following through.
examples: He planned our trip to Japan on date two — then never mentioned it again. Future faking.

entries.definition: Personal limits that define what you are comfortable with. Respecting them is a key green flag.
examples: Telling him I need a night alone each week was setting a healthy boundary.

entries.definition: Unable or unwilling to open up, be vulnerable or commit emotionally.
examples: He's charming, but emotionally unavailable.

entries.definition: Reliably showing up, following through and communicating in a steady way — a strong green flag.
examples: Her consistency made me feel safe.

entries.definition: Mutual give-and-take in effort, affection and interest.
examples: A relationship without reciprocity feels like talking to a wall.

entries.definition: Refusing to communicate or engage during a conflict, shutting the other person out.
examples: Every time we argue he stonewalls me for days.

entries.definition: An unhealthy pattern where one person's sense of self-worth depends excessively on taking care of, or pleasing, a partner.
examples: She realised that never spending time apart had become codependency.

entries.definition: An attachment style marked by comfort with closeness and independence, and trust in a partner.
examples: His secure attachment made the relationship feel calm.
entries.note: From attachment theory, developed by John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth.

entries.definition: An attachment style marked by a strong need for reassurance and a fear of abandonment.
examples: My anxious attachment kicks in when he takes hours to reply.

entries.definition: An attachment style marked by discomfort with closeness and a strong preference for independence.
examples: Whenever things got serious, his avoidant attachment made him pull away.

entries.definition: A strong, often secret and short-lived feeling of attraction toward someone.
examples: I've had a crush on him since the first day of school.

entries.definition: The fluttery, nervous-excited feeling in your stomach when you're near someone you like.
examples: I still get butterflies when she walks into the room.

entries.definition: A natural, mutual attraction and connection between two people.
examples: The chemistry between them was obvious to everyone.

entries.definition: The exciting feeling of attraction at the start of, or within, a romance.
examples: After twenty years of marriage, they still have the spark.

entries.definition: Deeply taken with or infatuated by someone.
examples: He's completely smitten with his new girlfriend.

entries.definition: An intense but often short-lived passion or admiration for someone.
examples: It felt like love, but it was really infatuation.

entries.definition: An involuntary state of intense romantic longing for someone, with obsessive thoughts and a desperate wish for the feelings to be returned.
examples: She replayed every conversation in her head — classic limerence.
entries.note: Coined by psychologist Dorothy Tennov in her 1979 book 'Love and Limerence'.

entries.definition: An intense but innocent romantic attachment, typically felt by young people.
examples: Their middle-school romance was sweet puppy love.

entries.definition: The experience of falling in love with someone the moment you first see them.
examples: He swears it was love at first sight.

entries.definition: A person you feel deeply and naturally connected to, as if meant to be together.
examples: After forty years together, she still calls him her soulmate.

entries.definition: A spiritual idea of an intense connection with someone believed to be your 'mirror soul'.
examples: She believes they're twin flames.

entries.definition: To be overwhelmed with adoration or romantic excitement; originally, to faint.
examples: The whole audience swooned at the proposal.

entries.definition: So in love, or longing so strongly, that it is hard to think of anything else.
examples: He moped around the house, completely lovesick.

entries.definition: Suddenly and completely overwhelmed by love.
examples: The lovestruck pair didn't notice the rain.

entries.definition: Overwhelming sadness and grief, especially after the loss of a love.
examples: Time and good friends helped her heal from the heartbreak.

entries.definition: A deep, persistent desire for someone, especially someone absent or out of reach.
examples: Her letters were full of longing.

entries.definition: An intense, often wistful longing.
examples: The song captured the yearning of first love.

entries.definition: To love and admire someone deeply.
examples: I adore the way you laugh.

entries.definition: Deep, loyal love and commitment.
examples: Their devotion to each other never wavered.

entries.definition: A gentle feeling of fondness and warmth toward someone.
examples: He showed his affection through little gestures.

entries.definition: Strong and intense romantic feeling or desire.
examples: Their passion was the talk of the village.

entries.definition: Close emotional familiarity and openness between people.
examples: Late-night talks built a deep intimacy between them.

entries.definition: Fear or resentment about losing someone's affection to another person.
examples: A little jealousy is human; controlling behaviour is not.

entries.definition: Firm belief in a partner's reliability, honesty and good intentions.
examples: Trust is built slowly and lost quickly.

entries.definition: The five ways people tend to give and receive love: words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service and physical touch.
examples: His love language is acts of service — he fixed my bike without being asked.
entries.note: Popularised by Gary Chapman's 1992 book 'The Five Love Languages'.

entries.definition: Completely and joyfully in love.
examples: She's head over heels for her new partner.

entries.definition: Gradually or suddenly developing romantic feelings for someone.
examples: I think I'm falling for you.

entries.definition: Feeling overwhelmed with attraction or emotion, as if your legs might give way.
examples: That smile makes me weak in the knees.

entries.definition: Full of dreamy, romantic and often idealistic hopes.
examples: The starry-eyed couple planned their whole future on the first date.

entries.definition: Felt or done equally by both people — as in mutual feelings or mutual attraction.
examples: Good news: the feeling is mutual.

entries.definition: Love that is not returned by the person you love.
examples: Poets have written about unrequited love for centuries.

entries.definition: Filled with love or strong admiration for someone.
examples: He was enamoured with her from their first conversation.

entries.definition: A Filipino word for the giddy, fluttery rush you feel when something romantic happens.
examples: When he held my hand, I felt pure kilig.

entries.definition: From the Yaghan language of Tierra del Fuego: a look shared by two people, each wishing the other would make the first move.
examples: Across the table there was a moment of mamihlapinatapai, and neither spoke.

entries.definition: A Brazilian Portuguese word for tenderly running your fingers through a loved one's hair.
examples: She fell asleep to his cafuné.

entries.definition: Norwegian and Danish for 'in love'; often used in English for the euphoria of first falling in love.
examples: Those first weeks, they were utterly forelsket.

entries.definition: To flatter or charm someone with kind and loving words, sometimes to persuade them.
examples: He sweet-talked her into another slice of cake.

entries.definition: An expression of praise or admiration. The best ones are specific and sincere.
examples: 'You make everyone feel welcome' is a compliment that lasts.

entries.definition: Excessive or insincere praise, often given to win favour.
examples: Flattery will get you everywhere — or so he hoped.

entries.definition: An affectionate nickname used for a romantic partner, such as 'honey' or 'darling'.
examples: Their pet name for each other is 'bean'.

entries.definition: A term of endearment for a loved one; also a romantic partner, as in 'high-school sweethearts'.
examples: They were high-school sweethearts who married at thirty.

entries.definition: A loving term of address for someone dear to you.
examples: 'Good morning, darling,' she whispered.

entries.definition: A sweet term of endearment for a partner or loved one.
examples: Honey, I'm home!

entries.definition: A casual, affectionate term for a romantic partner; also slang for an attractive person.
examples: Babe, have you seen my keys?

entries.definition: An attractive or endearing person.
examples: Who's the cutie in the yellow jacket?

entries.definition: Strikingly beautiful or attractive.
examples: You look absolutely gorgeous tonight.

entries.definition: So beautiful or impressive that it takes your breath away.
examples: She looked stunning in the red dress.

entries.definition: Delightful and pleasing in a way that attracts people.
examples: What a charming smile you have.

entries.definition: Glowing with happiness, health or beauty.
examples: She was radiant on her wedding day.

entries.definition: Looking visibly happy, healthy and full of life.
examples: You're glowing — whatever you're doing, keep doing it.

entries.definition: Wonderfully attractive or romantic, like something from a dream.
examples: The new barista is so dreamy.

entries.definition: A person, often a celebrity, whom many people find very attractive.
examples: He was the heartthrob of every '90s teen magazine.

entries.definition: Someone considered a highly desirable partner.
examples: Kind, funny and great with kids? She's a catch.

entries.definition: A person who is very pleasant to look at.
examples: The lifeguard was serious eye candy.

entries.definition: Informal for a very attractive person.
examples: Your brother is a total hottie.

entries.definition: Slang for an exceptionally attractive person.
examples: Did you see her date? Absolute smokeshow.

entries.definition: So romantic or attractive that it could make someone swoon.
examples: That rooftop proposal was swoon-worthy.

entries.definition: A short, affectionate written message to someone you love.
examples: She found a love note tucked in her lunch box.

entries.definition: A term of endearment for someone kind, gentle or beloved.
examples: Thank you for the soup, you're an angel.

entries.definition: To make a place feel happier and brighter simply by being there.
examples: Your smile could light up a room.

entries.definition: The period during which a couple develops a romantic relationship, traditionally leading to marriage.
examples: Their courtship lasted two summers of letters and picnics.

entries.definition: A boyfriend or male admirer. From French for 'handsome'.
examples: She arrived at the ball with her new beau.

entries.definition: A beautiful, admired woman, especially the most admired at an event. From French for 'beautiful'.
examples: She was the belle of the ball.

entries.definition: A person who pursues a relationship with someone, especially with marriage in mind.
examples: She had more suitors than she could count.

entries.definition: A lover, especially a secret or illicit one.
examples: The novel's heroine meets her paramour in the garden at midnight.

entries.definition: A song or piece of music performed for a loved one, traditionally outdoors at night beneath their window.
examples: He serenaded her with a guitar under the balcony.

entries.definition: An old-fashioned or poetic word for a young lover or suitor, especially one from the countryside.
examples: The lovesick swain wrote poems to the shepherdess.

entries.definition: Brave, courteous and attentive, especially toward a romantic interest.
examples: In a gallant gesture, he offered her his coat.

entries.definition: Courteous, respectful and considerate behaviour, originally the code of medieval knights.
examples: Holding the door was a small act of chivalry.

entries.definition: A person, traditionally a woman, who flirts playfully to win admiration rather than commitment.
examples: The coquette fluttered her fan and smiled at every gentleman.

entries.definition: A fashionable, charming but irresponsible man devoted to pleasure, especially in Regency-era stories.
examples: Everyone warned her about the handsome rake.

entries.definition: A man known for seducing many people. Named after the Venetian adventurer Giacomo Casanova (1725–1798).
examples: He's a real Casanova — a new date every week.

entries.definition: A passionate male lover or romantic, after the hero of Shakespeare's 'Romeo and Juliet'.
examples: Look at Romeo over there, buying roses for the whole table.

entries.definition: A man who seduces and deceives many people. After a character in Nicholas Rowe's 1703 play 'The Fair Penitent'.
examples: The village lothario had broken half the hearts in town.

entries.definition: A legendary Spanish seducer; used for any man who pursues many romantic conquests.
examples: He fancies himself a Don Juan.

entries.definition: The Roman god of love, often shown as a winged child whose arrows make people fall in love.
examples: Looks like Cupid's arrow finally hit you.

entries.definition: A sweetheart chosen or greeted on Saint Valentine's Day (14 February); also a card sent on that day.
examples: Will you be my Valentine?

entries.definition: A love letter. From French, literally 'sweet note'.
examples: He hid a billet-doux inside her favourite book.

entries.definition: A private, romantic meeting between lovers.
examples: They arranged a secret tryst by the old bridge.

entries.definition: A planned meeting at an agreed time and place, often romantic. From French 'present yourselves'.
examples: Our rendezvous is at eight, by the fountain.

entries.definition: A private, intimate conversation between two people. From French, literally 'head to head'.
examples: They slipped away for a quiet tête-à-tête on the balcony.

entries.definition: A person who historically accompanied an unmarried couple to ensure proper behaviour.
examples: Their aunt acted as chaperone at every dance.

entries.definition: A brief or casual romantic relationship.
examples: It was only a summer dalliance.

entries.definition: A love affair, especially a secret one; from the French word for love.
examples: Paris was the setting for their brief amour.

entries.definition: Great enthusiasm or passion, especially in love.
examples: He declared his ardour in a twelve-page letter.

entries.definition: Engaged to be married; also the person to whom one is engaged.
examples: She introduced her betrothed to the family.

entries.definition: To run away secretly to get married, often without the approval or knowledge of family.
examples: They eloped to Gretna Green in the middle of the night.

entries.definition: A mid-twentieth-century expression for dating someone exclusively.
examples: In 1958, going steady meant wearing his class ring.

entries.definition: A charming, funny or unlikely first meeting between future romantic partners, especially in films.
examples: Spilling coffee on each other at the airport was their meet-cute.

entries.definition: A couple who are openly and affectionately in love, named after small parrots that sit closely in pairs.
examples: The lovebirds held hands through the entire film.

entries.definition: Unhappy because of unrequited love or the absence of a loved one.
examples: The lovelorn poet wrote by candlelight.

entries.definition: Affectionate, often whispered, words of love that carry more feeling than meaning.
examples: He whispered sweet nothings as they danced.

entries.definition: To make someone fall in love with you.
examples: She stole his heart with one terrible joke.

entries.definition: To long intensely for someone, especially someone absent or out of reach.
examples: He spent the summer pining for her.

entries.definition: A much-loved person; dearly loved.
examples: He wrote every poem for his beloved.

entries.definition: A woman who is someone's lover or beloved; the male form is 'inamorato'. From Italian.
examples: The artist painted his inamorata again and again.

entries.word: Wear Your Heart on Your Sleeve
entries.definition: To show your feelings openly and honestly.
examples: He wears his heart on his sleeve — you always know how he feels.

entries.definition: A former romantic partner, especially one for whom feelings still linger.
examples: She ran into an old flame at the reunion.

entries.definition: A shy person who stays at the edge of a social event, originally someone without a dance partner.
examples: The wallflower turned out to be the best dancer in the room.
